title: Wet blocking
subtitle: Soaking a finished knit piece to set the stitches and the dimensions.
excerpt: Wet blocking submerges a knitted piece in water, lets the fibres relax and even out, then pins the piece to the stated dimensions while it dries. Essential for lace, woollen garments, and any piece where stitch definition matters.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), finishing chapter. Weldon's Practical Knitter finishing notes (1886). Standard wet-blocking practice documented across British and Scandinavian textile traditions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A finishing process in which a knitted piece is soaked in water, gently pressed to remove excess water, then pinned or shaped to the correct dimensions and left to dry.

content.text: is the standard finishing method for woollen knitwear. Water relaxes the fibres, allows the stitches to even out, and lets the piece be stretched to the exact dimensions the pattern specifies. Lace opens fully only after wet blocking. Garments gain their final drape and shape. Swatches give reliable measurements only after being wet-blocked. Difficulty: beginner.
A basin or sink large enough to hold the piece flat
Lukewarm water (cold for superwash wool and acrylics)
A foam blocking mat or clean flat surface

attrs.title: Fibre check
attrs.body: Wool and plant fibres (cotton, linen) wet-block well. Acrylic and nylon hold their shape without soaking; steam-blocking works better for those. Check your yarn label for washing guidance before submerging.

content.text: Fill the basin with lukewarm water. Submerge the piece and gently press it down until fully wet. Leave for 15-20 minutes.
Lift the piece out without wringing. Support the whole weight to avoid stretching the fibres while they are at their most delicate.
Lay the piece on a clean towel. Roll the towel up around the knitting and press firmly to absorb excess water. Unroll.
Transfer to the blocking mat. Lay flat and coax to the stated finished dimensions, pinning at regular intervals along the edges. Pin lace points individually.
Leave to dry fully, which may take several hours or overnight depending on thickness. Do not move the piece until it is completely dry.

Lace shawls, woollen garments, and Fair Isle yokes all need wet blocking to reach their stated dimensions. Any pattern with a finishing section that says 'block to measurements' means wet blocking unless it specifies otherwise.

items.cause: Water too hot, or the piece was agitated during soaking
items.fix: Use lukewarm water and handle the piece gently. Never rub, wring, or move it around in the water. Feltable wools (non-superwash) are particularly sensitive.

items.symptom: Piece still looks uneven after drying
items.cause: Not enough pins, or removed before fully dry
items.fix: Use more pins at closer intervals, especially on curved edges and lace points. Leave for a full night before unpin.

items.symptom: Piece returned to original shape once unpinned
items.cause: Acrylic or nylon yarn, which has memory that water cannot reset
items.fix: Steam blocking or the damp-towel method works better than wet blocking for synthetic fibres.
